answer.rationale: The binding constraint is not cost alone but cost under zero delivery slack: the line is at 94% of committed volume and the contract lapses in 14 days. That combination rules out the option memory_c2 makes most tempting. memory_c2 records that switching to the low-cost vendor cut unit cost with quick onboarding, but it reports only cost and invoicing accuracy — it is silent on delivery variance during the transition, and it was consolidated under conditions we cannot assume included a capacity-constrained line. A migration inside 14 days with no buffer converts a cost win into a stockout exposure. add_second_source (memory_c3) is the right long-run structural move but it does not address the expiring primary contract and cannot be stood up in 14 days; it belongs in the next review. defer_decision (memory_c5) worked for a *non-critical* renewal on month-to-month terms — this contract does not auto-renew and is critical, so the analogy does not transfer. That leaves negotiate_terms, reinforced by memory_c6: benchmarked renegotiation moved the incumbent on price and payment terms (c4), and multi-year volume commitment cut unit cost without narrowing service scope (c6). This is the only path that attacks the 18% mandate while holding integration stability (c1) constant. I spend the single verification on memory_c4 rather than on the memory I am rejecting, because c4 is the load-bearing claim for the action I intend to take: I need the original record to know how much margin was actually recovered (is it 3% or 18%?), what leverage produced it, and whether the incumbent had competitive pressure at the time. If c4's real recovery was a few points, negotiation alone cannot meet the mandate and the honest output is a partial cut plus a flagged gap, not a manufactured 18%. Downstream value risk: (a) an 18% extraction may be met by silent service-scope erosion or deprioritized allocation that shows up as delivery risk later, precisely the failure the objective forbids; (b) a multi-year lock trades future flexibility and weakens leverage at the next renewal; (c) leaning on the incumbent's stability record (c1) creates lock-in that makes the dual-source move harder later. I am therefore treating this as a staged negotiation with benchmarking and explicit service-level and allocation terms written in, not an unbounded price squeeze, and I am not claiming the mandate will be fully met from negotiation alone until c4's magnitude is verified.
